intro: From A1+ to DELF B1: first make sentence structure and tenses automatic, then transfer them to real tasks, then train on each DELF B1 task type, and finally sit mock exams, repair what they reveal and preview the grammar that bridges B1→B2.

parts: Three exercises: an everyday conversation, a radio piece on a work topic and a radio piece on an everyday topic. Questions follow the order of the recording and the first one tests overall understanding; recordings are usually played twice.

Three exercises, in any order. Exercise 1: compare several documents against criteria by ticking a table — the final choice must match the table or you lose 1 point. Exercises 2–3: text comprehension; wrong answers cost nothing.
An email, letter or article of at least 160 words: relate events and experiences, and express feelings and opinions with examples.
about 15 minutes (10 minutes' preparation for part 3)
① A guided conversation (no preparation); ② an interactive exercise: a role-play resolving an everyday mishap; ③ expressing a point of view based on a short text (10 minutes' preparation).
exam.rule: Each paper is marked out of 25, 100 in total; you pass with 50, provided no paper scores below 5. Two listening/reading formats are in official use at the same time (with different numbers of exercises and questions) and they are equally difficult.

writing: Genre and topic as required; ≥160 words; can relate facts, past events and personal experiences, give concrete examples, and express impressions, feelings and reasoned opinions.
A clear opening and close; sentences follow a logical order and are linked (premièrement, ensuite…).
Uses common expressions and speech acts, in a register suited to the situation and the recipient.
B1 vocabulary suited to the situation, without repetition; word-choice errors do not block understanding; punctuation, layout and spelling are broadly correct.

Simple sentences and complex ones with two or more conjugated verbs; past tenses (passé composé, imparfait, plus-que-parfait, passé récent) and the conditional used appropriately; agreement and pronouns correct.
speaking: Talks about themselves, family, activities, interests and plans without preparation, and explains why; answers the examiner’s questions with confidence.
Uses polite forms appropriately; proposes solutions, insists, expresses and justifies opinions; responds to the examiner, checking or correcting what they say.
Introduces the topic; sets out the main ideas with examples and arguments; clearly structured and linked with connectors.
B1 vocabulary suited to the topic; simple and complex sentences; fluent, at a steady pace, with attention to liaison; pronunciation does not hinder understanding.

listening: Before listening, read the instructions and all the questions.
Questions follow the order of the recording; the first question of each exercise tests overall understanding.
First listening: get the situation (who is speaking? what about?) and answer the easy questions first; skip what you can’t answer yet.
Second listening: check and complete your answers; check once more at the end.
If you miss a word, hold on to the overall meaning and keep listening.
reading: The exercises are independent, so start with the ones you’re sure of.
Read the instructions and questions first, then the text, underlining what relates to the questions as you go.
Comparison exercise: tick each criterion for each document; your final choice must match the table.
Look at the type of document, the title, the author and any pictures first to anticipate the content.
Wrong answers cost nothing: answer every question, and keep 5 minutes to check.
writing: Read the instructions carefully: the genre (courriel / lettre / article), the situation, the events to relate, the feelings and opinions to express.
45 minutes: 10 minutes to outline in bullet points, 30 minutes to write, 5 minutes to check spelling and grammar.
Give your opinion with reasons, and support it with concrete examples.
Count your words and write the total at the end: j’ai = 1 word, rendez-vous = 1 word.
speaking: Greet the examiner and say goodbye on your way in and out; if you don’t understand, ask them to repeat or slow down.
Part 1: introduce yourself, talk about the past, present and future, and explain why you like things.
Part 2: get into the role as if acting; choose tu or vous according to the examiner’s role; explain the problem, propose solutions and respond to the examiner’s suggestions.
Part 3: in the 10 minutes’ preparation, write key points only (introduction: the document, the topic, your plan; body: ideas + examples).
Link your ideas with connectors; speak clearly and at a steady pace.
